planting.note: Plant container-grown or divided stock in fall into rocky, well-drained foothill soil; seed has a hard double-dormant coat and is far slower and less reliable than starting from transplants.

directions: Roundleaf snowberry fills the shrub layer of the Gambel oak and mountain mahogany foothill belt, tucking into the dappled edges of oak thickets where few other natives tolerate the dry shade. Its small, rounded, blue-green leaves and pale pink bell flowers in early summer give way to chalky white berries that hang on well into winter, feeding grouse, deer mice, and songbirds after most other forage is gone. The plant spreads gradually by underground rhizomes to knit together loose, informal colonies useful for stabilizing foothill slopes and road cuts. It asks for almost nothing once established beyond occasional thinning of old wood, shrugging off drought, poor rocky soil, and browsing pressure alike.

planting.note: Seed has a rock-hard coat and needs a hot-water soak or mechanical scarification before fall sowing into gravelly, fast-draining foothill soil in full sun; untreated seed can sit dormant for years.

directions: Fendler's ceanothus is a low, wiry, spine-tipped shrub that threads through the open ground between Gambel oak clumps and mountain mahogany on dry foothill and lower montane slopes of the southern Rockies. Dense clusters of small white flowers smother the stiff branches in late spring and early summer, drawing in bees and butterflies, and the nitrogen-fixing nodules on its roots let it colonize thin, depleted rocky soil that defeats most other shrubs. Deer and elk browse it heavily in winter, and its tangled, thorny structure also provides cover for ground-nesting birds. Give it lean soil and full sun and resist the urge to irrigate or fertilize, both of which encourage weak growth and root rot.

subcategory: foothill and montane rock garden perennial

planting.note: Winter-sow outdoors or sow about two months before last frost with only a light dusting of soil over the seed; needs sharply drained, gravelly soil and resents sitting wet over winter.

directions: Despite its name, this penstemon is as much a foothill plant as a high-elevation one, lining dry rocky roadcuts and open shrubland gaps between Gambel oak stands from the base of the Front Range well up into the subalpine zone. Clusters of sky-blue, tubular flowers with white-and-purple-striped throats rise on reddish stems above a low rosette in late spring, taller and showier than the cushion-forming beardtongues that share its range. It is an easy, reliable native for a xeric border or rock garden, tolerating poor soil and reflected heat as long as drainage is sharp. Avoid rich or regularly irrigated beds, which shorten its lifespan considerably.

planting.note: A period of cold, moist stratification markedly improves and speeds germination; direct sow in fall or very early spring into humus-rich but well-drained soil in light shade.

directions: Pineywoods geranium grows along the leafy, slightly shaded margins where Gambel oak thickets meet ponderosa pine, a niche a little cooler and less baked than the open shrubland around it. Cup-shaped, pink-to-magenta flowers with darker veining appear over a long stretch from late spring through summer and are a steady draw for native bees. It wants a touch more organic matter and moisture retention than true xeric foothill shrubs but still fails in heavy, waterlogged soil. Left alone it spreads modestly by self-seeding and short rhizomes into a loose, long-blooming groundcover for a woodland-edge border.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed directly outdoors so natural winter cold and moisture break dormancy; seedlings emerge and leaf out very early the following spring, well before most neighboring shrubs.

directions: Geyer's larkspur is an early-spring ephemeral of foothill grasslands and the open gaps within Gambel oak and mountain mahogany shrubland, often finishing its entire above-ground cycle before summer heat sets in. Branched spikes of deep blue-purple spurred flowers rise above finely cut, deeply lobed leaves in April and May, among the first native wildflowers to color the foothills as the oak breaks dormancy. By the time the surrounding shrubs leaf out fully, the plant has set seed and died back to its deep taproot to wait out the dry season underground. All parts are toxic if eaten, as with other larkspurs, so site it away from grazing animals, livestock pasture, and curious pets.
